extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of ancient philosophy and moral philosophy (readers of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics)
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory notes and critical glosses on Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics focusing on definitions and evaluative standards for happiness, virtue, moral responsibility, and intellectual method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness partly dependent on conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness is not a mere direct gift from Heaven but comes at least partly from ourselves; if it were wholly given independently of conduct, there would be no motive to self-discipline and moral improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle argues that supposing happiness to come partly from our actions does not depreciate its value; it preserves motive for moral improvement and self-discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: No congenital incapacity for virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The commentator insists that what has been 'maimed was once perfect' — Aristotle does not contemplate a person born incapable of virtue and thus incapable of happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit normative claim: moral education and improvement are possible; evaluations of responsibility and virtue should not presuppose congenital incapacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness grounded in abiding cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Although people imagine Happiness should be abiding, fortune is changeable; therefore Aristotle bases Happiness on the most abiding cause so that the concept of Happiness aligns with stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether someone is happy, prefer criteria tied to long-lasting, abiding causes rather than merely transient goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: External goods proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: External abilities and goods are instruments of action and should be proportioned to the work or station; persons are 'blessed in worldly respects' who have what their station requires, even if no more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of a person's worldly blessedness or prosperity should measure whether their external instruments are fit for their role, not whether they are grand or ostentatious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of faculties depends on use
rubrics_metrics.description: Goods 'in posse' (faculties) are good only when rightly used; e.g., Rhetoric may be used to promote justice or abused to support villainy; money likewise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate faculties and talents by their exercised use — a skill or faculty is counted valuable only insofar as it is directed to the right ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-control vs incontinence distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The enkrates has bad or unruly appetites but reason strong enough to keep them under; the akrates is one whose appetites constantly prevail over reason and earlier resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral evaluations should distinguish persons who struggle but maintain control (enkrates) from those whose appetites consistently override reason (akrates); the law of habit pushes enkrates toward self-mastery and akrates toward perdition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-mastery = substituting reason for impulses
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-mastery is described by the Greek phrase meaning substituting that person's logos for one's own — the irrational nature in a self-controlled person substitutes the orders of Reason for its own impulses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify self-mastery by observable substitution of reasoned orders for impulsive inclinations; this is the sign of moral improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as regulation, not eradication, of passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue consists in the due regulation of all parts of our nature; passions are integral and have proper office — the aim is not their extirpation but their cultivation for right use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extremes: moral perfection is not emotional numbness but harmony achieved by habituation (analogy: turning discordant instruments into music rather than silencing them).

rubrics_metrics.name: Habits formed by action (praxis) not mere results (pragma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Praxis (action as process) forms habit, while pragma (mere result) does not; repetition of facts (pragmata) does not constitute the formation of moral habit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating moral formation, look to repeated intentional activities and processes rather than merely to outcomes or results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral responsibility tied to capacity for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A person is not responsible for being merely formed with certain propensions (theratos) but is responsible for being so far formed that they 'might have improved and raised himself to a higher and more secure state of virtue' (eutheratos) by contrary behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribution of moral blame depends on whether the agent had the capacity and opportunity to cultivate virtue by contrary action; moral evaluation must account for prior capacity and chance for improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue aligns with self-interest and duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is not only duty but also the interest of man: conscience and reasonable self-love are two principles which in fact lead the same course of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a course is virtuous, consider both its duty-bound character and its consonance with properly understood self-interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different ignorance types affect moral blame
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance of particular facts affects the rightness of the pragma (result), whereas ignorance that indicates an incapacity to discern principles shows a depraved moral constitution (conscience perverted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish inadvertent factual error from defective moral perception; the latter carries graver normative import for assessments of blameworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive as designed causation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greek eneka, primarily denoting cause-and-effect, comes to mean designed causation and motive; in the primary sense one cannot be ignorant of one's own motive of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral explanation and assessment should treat motives as intended or designed causation; claims of ignorance regarding one's motive require careful scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions, not opinions, establish habits/character
rubrics_metrics.description: On objects of moral choice, opinion is not the same as Moral Choice: actions alone form habits and constitute character; opinions are generally signs of character until acted upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge moral character solely from professed beliefs — give primacy to repeated choices and deeds as the genuine evidence of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for moral choice: reason and will alignment
rubrics_metrics.description: For every moral action (assuming uninjured mental machinery) Reason must have said 'Aye' when it ought and the Will must act accordingly; the will waits upon deliberation where Reason is judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral voluntariness by checking whether deliberation produced a rightful judgment and whether the will executed it; failure of either undermines moral voluntariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between akrasia and deliberate wrongdoing
rubrics_metrics.description: Faulty action arises either when the machinery is perfect but wrongly directed (deliberate crime) or when the direction given by Reason is right but the Will does not move accordingly (akrates — 'video meliora proboque, deteriora sequor').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate weakness of will (less culpable in some contexts) from outright deliberate vice; the explanation affects moral appraisal and possible remediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency limited to actions not circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Habits are formed by acting under certain circumstances; we can choose how we will act but not what circumstances we will have to act under.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral evaluation should take into account the agent's ability to change actions rather than circumstances; responsibility for habit formation rests on choices within constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for true courage
rubrics_metrics.description: True Courage requires (1) exact appreciation of danger and (2) a proper motive for resisting fear; spurious forms fail on one or both counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging acts as courageous, check both accuracy of risk assessment and the moral quality of the motivating end (e.g., honour vs rashness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for justice
rubrics_metrics.description: To make up the character of Justice a person must have the capacity, do the acts, and do them from moral choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims of justice by verifying ability, conduct, and volitional moral intent rather than mere compliance or external performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality as fairness test
rubrics_metrics.description: Fairness in reciprocation requires the same ratio between wares as between persons; proper distribution depends entirely on that first proportion (example: dividing profits in given ratios).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use proportionality (equality of ratios) as the standard when evaluating the fairness of exchanges or distributions rather than absolute comparisons alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injustice defined as violation of equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Every unjust act embodies to adikon, a violation of to ison (equality), implying a greater and a less share — injustice is diagnosed by unequal distribution of shares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying an injustice, look for a concrete inequality produced by the act (one party gains more at the expense of another).

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction's reliability depends on cognitive quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is a branch of probable reasoning; its validity depends entirely on the quality of the particular mind which performs it — rapid induction is a mark of genius and its certainty is subjective, not objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate inductive inferences by assessing the epistemic capacities and discernment of the reasoner, not merely by enumerative evidence alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for correct logical division
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of correct logical division is that the membra dividentia (dividing members) shall be opposed, i.e., not included one by the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a logical division or classification, ensure members are mutually exclusive and not overlapping inclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of popular language/coextensiveness in definition
rubrics_metrics.description: In some appeals to definition Aristotle and the commentator use popular language and tests of coextensiveness (predicating one thing of another to show coextensiveness) as part of proving an art or defining its boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating definitions or demonstrative proofs, consider ordinary-language usage and tests of coextensiveness as legitimate heuristic devices, but check for logical conversion as the proper test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposes of inquiry classify intellectual virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind attains truth either for the sake of truth itself (aplos) or for the sake of something further (eneka tinos); this distinction distinguishes types of intellectual activity (episteme, nous, sophia, phronesis, techne).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess intellectual achievements by their telos: whether they aim at pure knowledge or practical ends; different teloi instantiate different intellectual virtues and standards of adequacy.
